question: Can orchestral music evoke a place as well as a person?
intro: A gently moving clarinet line opens a portrait of an eighteenth-century house and its musical visitor. Woodwind exchanges and light strings keep the scene on a chamber scale.

sections.label: VIII · A house and its visitor

cues.title: A clarinet leads
cues.text: The opening melody belongs to the clarinet, with a lightly moving accompaniment below. Follow the line as other wind colours enter rather than treating every change of instrument as a new tune.
cues.evidence: Novello p. 47, rehearsal 30: clarinet melody above bassoon and low strings; subsequent wind exchanges appear in pp. 48–51.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Winifred Norbury and Sherridge
cues.text: Winifred Norbury is associated with the Worcestershire Philharmonic Society. Elgar says her portrait also concerns the eighteenth-century house Sherridge, where she lives; a suggestion of her laugh connects the place with its occupant.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society identifies Norbury, the society and the house; Elgar’s commentary describes the laugh. https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations

cues.title: A bridge towards Nimrod
cues.text: The score lets a first-violin note lead into Nimrod. This file ends before that next variation: listen to the quieter closing passage as a preparation rather than assuming the digital track boundary is Elgar’s intended pause.
cues.evidence: Novello p. 51 leads directly into p. 52. The report withdraws after 1:14 and falls markedly in its final windows. The separate source file cannot establish a continuous digital join.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: PDF pp. 47–51, rehearsal figures 30–32. Whole-variation passage map, using the report’s 0:14, 0:32, 0:52 and 1:14 changes and the final held-note span. The piccolo switch is read from the score.

timeline.note: Clarinet opens above moving low strings; the first upper-string entries come later in the phrase (p. 47).
Woodwind exchanges spread above the full string texture, with restrained horn support (pp. 47–48).
A lower-wind response and lighter strings momentarily change the balance of the conversation (pp. 48–49).
Piccolo briefly colours the upper wind line as the later phrase regains motion (pp. 49–50).
The wind and string phrase broadens and diminishes; the piccolo player has returned to flute (p. 51).
A held first-violin note remains after the other parts release, linking the written ending to Nimrod (last bar, p. 51).

composer.epithet: A Worcester violinist who made orchestral variations into portraits of friends and the concerto into an argument with memory.
facts: Largely self-taught; violin, organ, orchestral playing and his father’s Worcester music shop
Bandmaster, Worcester County Asylum, Powick, 1879–84 · organist, St George’s Catholic Church, 1885–89 · Master of the King’s Musick, 1924–34
Two completed symphonies; violin and cello concertos; choral works; chamber music; five completed Pomp and Circumstance marches
composer.background:
Elgar learned the orchestra from inside it. His father William kept a music shop in Worcester, tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church. Edward read the scores in the shop, played violin in local ensembles, taught several instruments and eventually succeeded his father at the organ. He was born in Lower Broadheath in 1857, a Catholic in a predominantly Anglican musical establishment and a tradesman’s son in a profession increasingly organised around London colleges. He remained sensitive to both distinctions throughout his later success. His practical education taught him how a phrase feels under a bow.

At Powick he wrote quadrilles and polkas for an unusual ensemble, learning to give each instrument useful work. The Three Choirs Festival brought larger repertory within reach: Handel, Mendelssohn and contemporary oratorio, alongside orchestral music from the Continent. Visits to London widened that education. Wagner mattered particularly: the chromatic connection between chords, the orchestral recollection of earlier events and the long postponement of a cadence all entered Elgar’s language. His mature scores acquired part of their English character through their subsequent public use.
